lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: One printout. One circled word. Forty-nine years of silence.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: August 15, 1977. A radio telescope in Ohio, listening for aliens, picks up something. It lasts exactly 72 seconds.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: Days later, a volunteer astronomer, Jerry Ehman, is reading the printout. He circles six characters, 6-E-Q-U-J-5, and writes one word beside them: "Wow!"

lines.speaker: moth
lines.text: That's it? That's the whole reaction?

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: The characters aren't a message. They're loudness, one character every 10 seconds. The U means about 30 times louder than background noise. It rose, peaked in the middle, and faded, which is how a real source in the sky should look.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: It sat near 1420 megahertz, the hydrogen line. Scientists had suggested that channel in 1959 as a sensible place to call another civilisation. It came from the direction of Sagittarius.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: Nobody has heard it again. Searches in 1987, 1989, 1995 and 1999 found nothing.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: Explanations: a reflected Earth signal, a one-off burst, a flickering signal. A 2017 comet idea was rejected by other astronomers. A 2024 preprint suggests a rare burst from a hydrogen cloud. Unconfirmed.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: Ehman said he would not draw "vast conclusions from half-vast data". Gloom: "Neither will I. Mostly."

scenes.caption: 6EQUJ5

scenes.visual: Dish sweeps empty sky, Biscuit stares up
scenes.caption: NEVER AGAIN

scenes.visual: Three speech bubbles, "?" stamped on each
scenes.caption: HALF-VAST DATA
